title: Micah 5:1–6
context: The prophet addresses Jerusalem under siege, where “the judge of Israel” is struck on the cheek, and then turns to Bethlehem Ephrathah, small among Judah’s clans, from which “one will come out to me who is to be ruler in Israel,” a shepherd who will stand “in the strength of the LORD” and be “our peace” against the Assyrian. Versification: English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14, and English 5:2–15 is Hebrew 5:1–14; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Both traditions read the promise in light of the covenant with David (2 Sam 7:12–16) as shared ground, and both name Matthew 2:5–6, where the chief priests and scribes cite this passage, without merging the two texts or pressing every detail of fulfillment.

verses.text: Now you shall gather yourself in troops, daughter of troops. He has laid siege against us. They will strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now you shall gather yourself in troops, daughter of troops. He has laid siege against us.” Arminian readers note that the prophet speaks to Jerusalem in a time of siege.

The striking of “the judge of Israel” on the cheek pictures humiliation of the city’s ruler.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse as distress before the promise of 5:2, and some also recall the striking of Jesus (cf. Matt 27:30), a link held with care.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the low point from which the hope of a new ruler rises.

verses.text: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me who is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings out are from of old, from ancient times.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, being small among the clans of Judah, out of you one will come out to me who is to be ruler in Israel.” Arminian readers note that the ruler comes from David’s town (cf. 1 Sam 16:1).

God raises greatness from what is small.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the promise to David’s house carried forward (cf. 2 Sam 7:12–16).

Shared ground: both traditions name Matthew 2:5–6 and John 7:42, and read “whose goings out are from of old” either as ancient Davidic origins or as the ruler’s eternal origin, holding the details with care.

verses.text: Therefore he will abandon them until the time that she who is in labor gives birth. Then the rest of his brothers will return to the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore he will abandon them until the time that she who is in labor gives birth.” Arminian readers note that a time of distress comes before the promised birth.

The woman may be Zion in labor (cf. 4:9–10) or the ruler’s mother, and readers hold both views.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise weigh these readings, and many connect the verse with Isaiah 7:14 while letting Micah’s wording stand.

Shared ground: both traditions read the return of “the rest of his brothers” as hope for a reunited people.

verses.text: He shall stand, and shall shepherd in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God. They will live, for then he will be great to the ends of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He shall stand, and shall shepherd in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God.” Arminian readers note the shepherd-king who rules by God’s strength.

His greatness reaches “to the ends of the earth.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a ruler whose authority comes from the LORD.

Shared ground: both traditions hear the Davidic shepherd theme (cf. Ezek 34:23) and read the promise of life under him as security under God’s chosen king.

verses.text: He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land and when he marches through our fortresses, then we will raise against him seven shepherds, and eight leaders of men.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land.” Arminian readers note that the ruler himself is the people’s peace.

The “seven shepherds, and eight leaders” may be a poetic way of saying enough and more, though its exact sense is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the ruler as the source of security, and some connect the phrase with Ephesians 2:14, a link held lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions read Assyria as the threat of Micah’s own day, while seeing a hope that reaches beyond it.

verses.text: They will rule the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in its gates. He will deliver us from the Assyrian, when he invades our land, and when he marches within our border.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will rule the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in its gates.” Arminian readers note that Nimrod’s land recalls Genesis 10:8–11.

The ruler “will deliver us from the Assyrian.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see deliverance from the great power of the day.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a promise of rescue framed in the terms of Micah’s world, without building a detailed timetable on it.
